passages.happening:
The dragon stood on the shore at the end of chapter 12. Now John sees what comes out of the sea: “Then I saw a beast with ten horns and seven heads rising out of the sea. There were ten royal crowns on its horns and blasphemous names on its heads” (verse 1).

“The beast I saw was like a leopard, with the feet of a bear and the mouth of a lion. And the dragon gave the beast his power and his throne and great authority” (verse 2).

“One of the heads of the beast appeared to be mortally wounded. But the mortal wound was healed, and the whole world marveled and followed the beast” (verse 3). People worship the dragon and the beast, saying, “Who is like the beast, and who can wage war against it?” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
The dragon now finds his instruments. In this chapter there are two beasts. The Greek word, thērion, means a wild animal. Where Christ is the Lamb, the powers set against God are beasts, violent and devouring. The word comes sixteen times in this chapter, as ‘throne’ filled chapter 4.

The first beast looks like the dragon: ten horns and seven heads. It wears royal crowns and ‘blasphemous names’, titles that claim for a human ruler what belongs to God. In John's world, emperors bore titles that Jews and Christians could only hear as blasphemy. Augustus was called ‘the one to be revered’, many emperors were called ‘son of the deified one’, and Suetonius reports that Domitian had official letters begin ‘our Lord and God’.

The beast is a mixture of Daniel's four beasts, lion, bear, leopard and the beast with ten horns, all rolled into one. In Daniel each beast was an empire. John's beast is imperial power as such. And it gets its authority from the dragon: ‘his power and his throne and great authority’.

Then comes a parody of the gospel. One head ‘appeared to be mortally wounded’, but was healed. The words are the same words used of the Lamb ‘who appeared to have been slain’ (5:6). The beast imitates the Lamb's death and rising, and the world is amazed and follows it.

And the world's question, ‘Who is like the beast?’, mocks Israel's song at the sea, ‘Who is like You, O LORD?’, and mocks the name of Michael, which means ‘Who is like God?’ The world's creed is that power proves itself: who can fight it? Amazement turns into worship.
passages.ot:
The beast rises like Daniel's: “Then four great beasts came up out of the sea, each one different from the others” (Daniel 7:3). The first “was like a lion” (Daniel 7:4), the second “looked like a bear” (Daniel 7:5), the third “was like a leopard” (Daniel 7:6), and the fourth “had ten horns” (Daniel 7:7).

And the world's cry turns Israel's praise upside down: “Who among the gods is like You, O LORD? Who is like You—majestic in holiness, revered with praises, performing wonders?” (Exodus 15:11).
passages.hard:
Who is the beast? Is it a nation, a ruler, or something in our own day?

Christians read the beast in the four ways the book page sets out, and these notes do not choose. Preterists and many others see Rome, whose governors and power came across the sea to Asia; Revelation 17:9 later ties the seven heads to seven hills, and Rome was famous as the city on seven hills. Historicist readers have often matched the beast with rulers and churches of their own times. Futurists generally expect a final ruler still to come. Idealists see the beast as a pattern that comes back in every age: state power that demands worship.

The healed head is read in more than one way too. Nero took his own life in AD 68, and civil war followed. Rumours spread that Nero had not died and would return from the east; Tacitus and Suetonius report men who claimed to be him. Many interpreters think the healed head plays on that rumour. Others take the wound as the empire's near collapse in 68 and 69, or as a parody of the resurrection and nothing more.

Christian history is full of confident readings that tied the beast to a figure of the reader's own day, and all of them were wrong. These notes identify the beast with no nation, leader, government, church, office or movement of our own time. The chapter's call is not to guess, but to see through any power that claims the worship due to God, and to refuse it.
passages.asks: Ask what kinds of power you are most tempted to admire or fear. Ask where you have heard the world's creed, ‘who can fight it?’, and believed it. And ask how a counterfeit of Christ might look convincing in your own setting.

passages.t: The beast wars against the saints
passages.happening:
“The beast was given a mouth to speak arrogant and blasphemous words, and authority to act for 42 months” (verse 5). It speaks against God, slanders his name “and His tabernacle—those who dwell in heaven” (verse 6).

“Then the beast was permitted to wage war against the saints and to conquer them, and it was given authority over every tribe and people and tongue and nation” (verse 7).

“And all who dwell on the earth will worship the beast—all whose names have not been written from the foundation of the world in the Book of Life belonging to the Lamb who was slain” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Notice the small word again: ‘given’, and ‘permitted’. It comes four times in this chapter. Even at its most arrogant, the beast acts only inside limits God has drawn, and for a time God has numbered: 42 months. That is the same three and a half years as in chapters 11 and 12, Daniel's figure for a season of trouble that is real and cut short.

The beast attacks God's name and God's ‘tabernacle’, his dwelling, and the verse explains that his dwelling is his people.

Then the hardest line: the beast is permitted ‘to wage war against the saints and to conquer them’. Revelation does not promise the church outward success against the beast. In the beast's courts, the saints lose, by being killed. In God's reckoning, the same faithfulness is their victory (12:11). Both are true at once.

The beast claims ‘every tribe and people and tongue and nation’, the very peoples the Lamb bought with his blood (5:9). And the line is drawn through humanity. Those whose names are in ‘the Book of Life belonging to the Lamb who was slain’ do not worship the beast.

Verse 8 holds a choice that translations make differently. ‘From the foundation of the world’ can go with ‘written’, as the BSB takes it, so that names were written in the book before the world began; 17:8 has nearly the same sentence and means that. Or it can go with ‘the Lamb who was slain’, as the King James Version and the NIV take it, so that the Lamb's sacrifice was set before the world began. Either way, God's purpose stands before history. The verse is meant to steady the persecuted, not to make anyone anxious.
passages.ot:
The beast's mouth is the mouth of Daniel's little horn: “a mouth that spoke words of arrogance” (Daniel 7:8). Daniel saw that “this horn was waging war against the saints and prevailing against them” (Daniel 7:21), until the Ancient of Days came and judgment was given for them. And the time is Daniel's: “the saints will be given into his hand for a time, and times, and half a time” (Daniel 7:25).

The three and a half years go back to the persecution under Antiochus IV, whose officials set up a pagan altar on the temple's altar in December 167 BC. The temple was dedicated again about three years later, in December 164 BC. A known crisis of limited length became the pattern of every persecution God allows, and also ends.
passages.asks: Ask how you would hold on if faithfulness looked, for a time, like losing. Ask what it means to you that the beast's power is ‘given’ and limited. And ask whether you find comfort or fear in the Book of Life, and why the verse means it as comfort.

passages.t: A call for perseverance and faith
passages.happening:
John steps out of the vision and speaks to his hearers directly, as the seven letters did: “He who has an ear, let him hear” (verse 9).

“‘If anyone is destined for captivity, into captivity he will go; if anyone is to die by the sword, by the sword he must be killed.’ Here is a call for the perseverance and faith of the saints” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
‘He who has an ear, let him hear’ is the refrain of the seven letters. Here it comes without ‘what the Spirit says to the churches’, as if the whole church is being spoken to at once.

The saying tells believers what to expect under the beast, and how to meet it. Some will be taken captive. Some will be killed. And the answer is ‘the perseverance and faith of the saints’.

The word for perseverance, hupomonē, means patient endurance, literally remaining under a load. John called himself a partner in it (1:9). And ‘faith’ here means both trust and faithfulness: loyalty that holds under pressure. The saints do not answer the beast with its own weapons. They do not take up the sword. And they do not give in. They endure, and they trust God with the outcome.

Jesus walked this road first. When the devil offered him the kingdoms of the world in exchange for worship, he refused: “Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only.” And when Peter drew a sword to defend him, Jesus said, “Put your sword back in its place” (Matthew 26:52).
passages.ot:
The saying comes from Jeremiah: “Those destined for death, to death; those destined for the sword, to the sword; those destined for famine, to famine; and those destined for captivity, to captivity” (Jeremiah 15:2). In Jeremiah it announced judgment on unfaithful Judah. John turns it into a word for the faithful, who must accept what the beast does to them.

And Daniel's friends showed the stance this verse asks for: “But even if He does not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden statue you have set up” (Daniel 3:18).
passages.hard:
Why does the King James Version read this verse differently? And does it ask believers to accept death?

Verse 10 is one of the most uncertain verses in Revelation in the old copies. The older text, which the BSB prints, reads it as a word about what believers must accept: captivity, or death by the sword. Most later copies, followed by the King James Version, read the second half as a warning: ‘he that killeth with the sword must be killed with the sword’, like Jesus' word to Peter (Matthew 26:52). On either reading, the saints do not take up the beast's weapons.

The verse honours believers who suffer for their faith. It does not ask anyone to seek death or to put themselves in harm's way. It asks them not to deny Christ, and not to answer violence with violence, when suffering comes.

Not every hardship comes from following Jesus, and not every hardship is meant to be endured in silence. If you are carrying something heavy, whether persecution, illness, loss, or harm at the hands of others, it is right to seek help and safety. Please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor. If you are in danger, or the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask what ‘perseverance and faith’ would look like in the pressures you face now. Ask whether you are tempted to answer hostility with its own weapons. And ask how you can pray for and stand with Christians who are imprisoned or killed for their faith today.

passages.happening:
“Then I saw another beast rising out of the earth. This beast had two horns like a lamb, but spoke like a dragon” (verse 11). It uses all the authority of the first beast and makes the world worship the first beast, “whose mortal wound had been healed” (verse 12).

It performs great signs, “to cause even fire from heaven to come down to earth in the presence of the people” (verse 13). By these signs it deceives the world, and tells people “to make an image to the beast that had been wounded by the sword and yet had lived” (verse 14).

“The second beast was permitted to give breath to the image of the first beast, so that the image could speak and cause all who refused to worship it to be killed” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
The second beast rises from the land. It looks harmless, with ‘two horns like a lamb’. The word for lamb is the word used for Christ throughout the book. But it speaks with the dragon's voice. Later Revelation calls it ‘the false prophet’ (16:13).

It does not ask for worship for itself. Its whole task is to turn people's worship toward the first beast. That is what makes it dangerous. It is religion put in the service of power, and counterfeit worship can look like a lamb.

In the province of Asia, the worship of the emperor was run by local people, not imposed from Rome. A provincial council organised festivals. Its high priests, from wealthy families, presided over temples and games. Acts mentions officials called Asiarchs at Ephesus, from this same provincial elite. A respectable local establishment made loyalty to Rome feel like piety.

The second beast works signs, even calling down fire from heaven, as Elijah did. Signs do not prove that a message is true. The Law tested a prophet by where his sign led, and Jesus warned that false prophets would perform signs to deceive.

Then the image is given ‘breath’, so that it seems alive and can speak, a mockery of God breathing life into the first human. And those who refuse to worship it are killed. Here the church's refusal becomes a matter of life and death.

About AD 112 Pliny the Younger, governor of Bithynia, on Asia's northern border, wrote to the emperor Trajan about how he tested people accused of being Christians. He had the emperor's image brought in with the statues of the gods, and required the accused to offer incense and wine to it and to curse Christ. Those who kept confessing Christ were put to death. The letter is some twenty years later than the usual date of Revelation, but it shows the very test this vision describes.
passages.ot:
The fire from heaven imitates Elijah on Mount Carmel: “Then the fire of the LORD fell and consumed the sacrifice” (1 Kings 18:38). The second beast is a counterfeit Elijah.

The Law had already warned about such signs: “If a prophet or dreamer of dreams arises among you and proclaims a sign or wonder to you, and if the sign or wonder he has spoken to you comes about, but he says, ‘Let us follow other gods’” then “you must not listen to the words of that prophet or dreamer” (Deuteronomy 13:1-3).

And the image that must be worshipped is Nebuchadnezzar's: “you must fall down and worship the golden statue that King Nebuchadnezzar has set up. And whoever does not fall down and worship will immediately be thrown into the blazing fiery furnace” (Daniel 3:5-6).
passages.hard:
Paul says that governing authorities are appointed by God (Romans 13:1). How can Revelation show a state receiving its power from the dragon?

The two chapters are not in contradiction. Paul writes, “there is no authority except that which is from God” (Romans 13:1), of government that serves justice; such a government acts as God's servant. Revelation shows a power that demands worship and makes war on God's people; such a power has become the dragon's instrument. The scholar Oscar Cullmann, in The State in the New Testament (1956), set the two texts side by side as the New Testament's two faces of the state.

These notes apply the picture of the second beast to no government, church, leader, office or movement of our own time. The test the chapter gives is for every reader to apply to himself first: what powers do I serve, and what does my religion end up blessing?
passages.asks: Ask where religion in your own world is used to make loyalty to power feel holy. Ask whether you are impressed by signs and success more than by faithfulness. And ask what it would cost you to refuse to bow to an image that everyone else honours.

passages.happening:
“And the second beast required all people small and great, rich and poor, free and slave, to receive a mark on their right hand or on their forehead, so that no one could buy or sell unless he had the mark—the name of the beast or the number of its name” (verses 16-17).

Then John speaks to his hearers again: “Here is a call for wisdom: Let the one who has insight calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and that number is 666” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
The pairs, small and great, rich and poor, free and slave, are a way of saying ‘everyone’.

The mark is the counterpart of God's seal. In chapter 7 God's servants were sealed on their foreheads. Israel was told to bind God's commands on the hand and the forehead. So the mark on the hand and forehead shows whose you are, and what governs your thinking and your doing.

Marks of belonging were familiar in John's world. Slaves could be branded, soldiers were sometimes marked, and devotees of certain gods bore their god's sign. The Greek word for mark, charagma, was used for the official stamp on documents and for the image pressed into coins, which bore the emperor's likeness and titles. And verse 17 explains the mark itself: it is ‘the name of the beast or the number of its name’.

Here the religious demand becomes an economic one. Without the mark, ‘no one could buy or sell’. In Asia, trade guilds, through which many people earned their living, held banquets under the patronage of gods, and refusing to take part could cost a believer customers and standing. The letters to Thyatira and Laodicea already raised this question. Worship shows up in the marketplace.

Then the number. In Greek and Hebrew, letters also served as numbers, so every name had a value, and working it out was a known game. A scratching on a wall at Pompeii says the writer loves a woman ‘whose number is 545’. John says the number of the beast can be calculated, and the Greek verb means to count with pebbles. That is why most interpreters think he expected his first hearers to be able to work it out.
passages.ot:
The mark on the hand and forehead is the dark mirror of God's command to Israel: “Tie them as reminders on your hands and bind them on your foreheads” (Deuteronomy 6:8).

Some readers also connect the number with Solomon, at the point where Israel's king began to trust in wealth: “The weight of gold that came to Solomon each year was 666 talents” (1 Kings 10:14).
passages.hard:
What is the mark of the beast, and what does 666 mean?

The mark is the counterpart of God's seal (7:3). Both show whom a person belongs to. Whether John meant a literal mark or a picture of allegiance, his first hearers knew what it was to be marked as someone's property, and they knew that loyalty to the emperor's gods could decide whether a person could trade. These notes tie the mark to no object, document, technology, payment, medicine or practice of our own day. Such claims have been made many times, and they have frightened many people. The chapter's own concern is worship and allegiance: whom you serve.

The number has been read in two main ways, and these notes do not choose. The first reads it as a name worked out by letter values. Irenaeus, about AD 180, weighed several names and declined to decide. The best-known solution is Nero: the name ‘Nero Caesar’ written in Hebrew letters adds up to 666. Some early copies read 616, among them a papyrus from Oxyrhynchus and a fifth-century codex, and the Latin spelling of the same name, without the final n, adds up to 616, which would explain that reading. Many interpreters, especially preterists, think John meant Nero. The second reads 666 as a symbol. Six falls short of seven, the number of completeness, so 666 is falling short three times over: a human power that always falls short of the God it claims to be. Some note that the name Jesus in Greek adds up to 888. Others link the number with Solomon's 666 talents of gold.

Christian history is full of confident attempts to fit 666 to someone in the reader's own day, and all of them were wrong. These notes make none. John calls for ‘wisdom’, and wisdom here is not guessing but discernment: to see what a power really is behind its claims, and to refuse it the worship that belongs to God.

Some readers are afraid that they have taken the mark without knowing it. In Revelation the mark goes with worshipping the beast and its image (14:9). The chapter speaks of allegiance, of whom a person chooses to worship. If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask where faithfulness to Christ costs you, or might cost you, at work or in the market. Ask whose ‘mark’ governs your thinking and your doing: your hand and your forehead. And ask whether you are more curious about decoding the number than about refusing the worship it stands for.
